    Important Words
    • icchantīm — looking for (one who wishes)
      Present participle of √iṣ — desiring. Arjuna correctly reads the tapas-posture as an icchā (desire) for a husband — a recognised motive for women's penance in śāstra (cf. Pārvatī, Sāvitrī).
    • patim — a husband
      Accusative of pati. The frame of the whole episode: Kālindī seeks a husband, and only One will do. Gauḍīyas: pati can mean simply 'husband' or 'Lord'; she chooses the word that admits both readings simultaneously.
    • kathaya — please explain
      Imperative of √kath. Arjuna's tone is courtly, not interrogative. The Bhāgavatam models how to address a tapasvinī — with respect, with space, with the request to speak rather than the demand.
    • śobhane — O beautiful one
      Vocative — a respectful epithet, not a flirtation. Kṣatriya etiquette toward a strange woman in penance: name her beauty as Lakṣmī-aṁśa, not as object.
    [Arjuna said:] Who are you, O fine-waisted lady? Whose daughter are you, and where do you come from? What are you doing here? I think you must be looking for a husband. Please explain everything, O beautiful one.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Arjuna said:] Who are you, O fine-waisted lady? Whose daughter are you, and where do you come from? What are you doing here? I think you must be looking for a husband. Please explain everything, O beautiful one.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Who are you--are you a devatā or human being and what is your name? Whose daughter are you? From which place (kutaḥ) have you come--where do you live? Or, for what purpose (kutaḥ) are you here? What do you desire to do? You are unmarried. I think that you desire to have a husband. You are most beautiful (suśroṇī)! You have the best qualities (suśobhane). You desire a husband with similar qualities. Arjuna saw her as a sister. When he says she has fine hips (varārohām) in the previous verse, it is only with that intention. Please reply to all my questions. Instead of sarvam sometimes kanyām is seen. Another meaning of suśobhane is “You should speak in a beautiful manner.”

    Important Words
    • savituḥ — of Savitā (the sun-god)
      Sūrya — the visible Sun. Kālindī's father is the sun-god; her sister is Yamī (Yamunā), her brother is Yamarāja. A cosmic lineage. Gauḍīyas: every great river is daughter of light; she chooses the source of light.
    • viṣṇum — Lord Viṣṇu
      She names her desired husband as Viṣṇu — the Bhāgavatam uses the name to signal her doctrinal clarity. Gauḍīya reading: she knows the Person she wants; the tapas is method, not search.
    • vara - dam — the bestower of boons
      Compound vara (boon) + da (giver). Kṛṣṇa is not merely the goal; He is the giver of the boon by which He becomes the goal. Gauḍīya: bhakti itself is His gift; the tapas works only because He has consented to be its fruit.
    • tapaḥ — penance
      From √tap — to heat. Penance burns away every desire except the one. Kālindī's tapaḥ is the long heat that has clarified her wish to a single point. Gauḍīyas: ekāgra-tapas is the prelude to ekāgra-bhakti.
    Śrī Kālindī said: I am the daughter of the sun-god. I desire to get as my husband the most excellent and munificent Lord Viṣṇu, and to that end I am performing severe penances.
    Purport

    As Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī points out, Śrīmatī Kālindī correctly understood that Lord Viṣṇu, being the source of all benedictions, is the supreme husband and can thus fulfill all the desires of His wife.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda

    "Desiring beautiful Visnu, who can fulfill my desires, as my husband, I am doing penance."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She reveals her desire immediately, worrying he would suggest someone other than her desired man. Out of respect she describes her father as devasya. This indicates she is also a devatā. I desire as a husband only he who spreads himself everywhere (viṣṇum), who is the best, and who bestows all desires.

    Analogy

    The Sun's own daughter sets her gaze on the One who is the Sun's source — water seeking its origin, light seeking the Lamp. Kālindī's penance is the cosmos' own reflex.

    Stories
    Sītā's choice

    Sītā, daughter of the earth, did not survey suitors at her svayaṁvara so much as wait for Rāma to lift the bow that none other could lift (Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa). Her vow was as firm as Kālindī's: this one or none.

    Gauḍīyas read the pattern: Lakṣmī-tattva, in each yuga's līlā, refuses every other husband. Kālindī's tapas is one more verse in that long śloka.

    Important Words
    • vṛṇe — will I choose
      From √vṛ — to choose. The same verb-root as svayaṁvara (the self-choice). Kālindī performs a private svayaṁvara of one: she has already chosen, and the river-house is her waiting room.
    • śrī — goddess of fortune
      In the compound śrī-niketanam — abode of Śrī. Kṛṣṇa is where Lakṣmī lives. Gauḍīyas: Lakṣmī's chosen abode is the heart-test; whoever Lakṣmī chooses is the rightful Lord.
    • mukundaḥ — Mukunda (Kṛṣṇa)
      The liberator. Kālindī names Him three different ways across these verses — Viṣṇu, Mukunda, Acyuta — exhausting the names of Bhagavān. Gauḍīya: each name is a different facet of the same Person; her devotion is theologically literate.
    • anātha - saṁśrayaḥ — the shelter of the helpless
      Compound anātha (without master) + saṁśraya (shelter). Kālindī claims helplessness — she has no other refuge. Gauḍīya śaraṇāgati: kārpaṇya (acknowledgement of one's helplessness) is the sixth and key limb.
    I will accept no husband other than Him, the abode of the goddess of fortune. May that Mukunda, the Supreme Personality, the shelter of the helpless, be pleased with me.
    Purport

    The beautiful Kālindī here reveals some apprehension. She insists that she will not accept any husband except Lord Kṛṣṇa, and she states that He is the shelter for those who have no other master. Since she will accept no other shelter, Kṛṣṇa must give her shelter. Also, she says, tuṣyatāṁ me sa bhagavān: “May that Supreme Lord be pleased with me.” This is her prayer. As Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī points out, although Kālindī is a young, helpless girl staying in a secluded place, she is not afraid. This staunch faith in and devotion for Lord Kṛṣṇa is ideal Kṛṣṇa consciousness, and Śrīmatī Kālindī’s desire will soon be fulfilled.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    I will accept no husband other than Him, the abode of the goddess of fortune. May that Mukunda, the Supreme Personality, the shelter of the helpless, be pleased with me.
    Commentary

    Worrying, she spoke , to negate any other person as her husband. "Visnu is the shelter of those without a master. Visnu is the master of his devotees and their protector. With this faith I live alone, though just a young girl, and do not fear other men."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Lakṣmī always remains on his chest out of prema. Or he gives shelter to even Lakṣmī who shelters wealth. Who would not accept him? Or he is the shelter of all wealth. This excluded others such as Brahmā and Śiva. O hero of dharma! I do not desire anything else. “But he is rarely achieved.” But he will accept me because he is affectionate to the miserable. May he be pleased with me since he is endowed with all qualities like compassion (bhagavān) and delivers everyone from suffering (mukundaḥ). Moreover he is the shelter for those with no other master. Or even though he is the Supreme Lord (bhagavān), may he be pleased with me since he is the shelter of those with no master. “Why do you have such determination for him?” He will free me from misery by freeing me from other desires (mukundaḥ). Or, he is Kṛṣṇa, manifesting directly all unlimited powers (bhagavān). Being the shelter of those with no master, he alone gives the best results even to the demons, giving them liberation (mukundaḥ). He is thus better than the Lords of Vaikuṇṭha. The conversation between Yamarāja and Yamunā is also rejected as contradictory. evaṁ vadanti rājarṣe ṛṣayaḥ ke ca nānvitāḥ yat sva-vāco virudhyeta nūnaṁ te na smaranty uta Such is the account given by some sages, O wise King, but those who speak in this illogical way are contradicting themselves, having forgotten their own previous statements. SB 10.77.30 There are two forms of Yamunā. One is the direct form who is the consort of the Lord and the other is the shadow form who is the wife of the ocean. The consort form stays in Dvārakā. The shadow form was pulled by Balarāma and then praised him. If this had been Kṛṣṇa’s eternal consort, it would mean a frightful afterlife for the Lord who appears to protect dharma.

    Important Words
    • kālindī — Kālindī
      Her name — derived from the Kalinda mountain whence Yamunā flows. Naming herself, she names the river she is rooted in. Gauḍīya: in Vraja, Kālindī is one of Yamunā's epithets; the wife of Kṛṣṇa shares her name with His beloved river.
    • yamunā - jale — in the water of the Yamunā
      Compound — locative. Her dwelling is inside the river itself, in a mansion her father built. Gauḍīyas read this as cosmic propriety: a child of the Sun dwells under the water her sister keeps.
    • acyuta - darśanam — the sight of Acyuta (Kṛṣṇa)
      Compound acyuta + darśana. The whole tapas is for darśana — and darśana of the acyuta specifically, the Lord who never falls away once seen. Gauḍīya: once Kṛṣṇa's darśana is granted, the bhakta is acyuta-darśanā forever.
    • yāvat — until
      A small word carrying her vow's whole structure: she will not stir from the water until darśana comes. Gauḍīya: niṣṭhā — fixed firmness — is the stage of bhakti between ruci and bhāva.
    I am known as Kālindī, and I live in a mansion my father built for me within the water of the Yamunā. There I will stay until I meet Lord Acyuta.
    Purport

    Since Kālindī was a beloved child of the sun-god himself, who would dare disturb her? From this incident we can appreciate the beautiful spiritual processes executed in previous ages by great souls. Unlike the so-called love in worldly “love affairs,” beautiful Kālindī’s love for Lord Kṛṣṇa was pure and perfect. Even though Kālindī was a tender young girl, her determination to marry Kṛṣṇa was so strong that she arranged for her father to build her a house in the Yamunā where she could perform severe austerities until the day her beloved came.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    I am known as Kālindī, and I live in a mansion my father built for me within the water of the Yamunā. There I will stay until I meet Lord Acyuta.
    Commentary

    "I am well known as Kalindi. Who does not know me, the daughter of the sun god?" By this statement she indicates her high status. "My father built me a house in the river. I am greatly favored by my father. Who has the power to go against me?"

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She then answers the questions. Kālindī means Yamunā. I am known as Kālindī and live in the water, filled with my energy. “Your living in the water means that you travel around everywhere like the fish.” I live in a house build by my father, the sun god, by some special powers. The sun is inconceivably able to move everywhere by his desire. Out of affection he made the best house for me. But I am not bewildered by this luxury. I will stay here until I am accepted by Kṛṣṇa, who never fails to keep his promise (acyuta). On seeing him and being accepted, my austerities will bear fruit. Simply staying and performing austerities is not my goal.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She then answers the questions. Kālindī means she is the figurative daughter of Kalinda Mountain (since Yamunā River arises from that mountain). This is my name (samākhyatā). Other names like Kṛṣṇā are secondary. Why do you live in the water? I live there in a palace built by my father. This answers the question kutaḥ (where). Since my father was the best of devatās, he could build the house in the water. Thus it was excellent, built out of affection. In that place I am not bewildered. The goal of my austerities is to see the Lord, who does not deviate from his promise (acyuta). Na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśyati: I declare that my devotee will not be vanquished. (BG 9.31)

    • guḍākeśaḥ — Arjuna (the conqueror of sleep)
      Compound guḍākā (sleep) + īśa (master). Arjuna is alert by epithet — and yet here he reports news to the One who never sleeps. Gauḍīyas: the master of sleep serves the eternal awake.
    • vidvān — already aware
      Past participle of √vid — knowing. The verse openly admits Kṛṣṇa already knew. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān is sarvajña; bhakti's information-flow is not for His update but for His relish.
    • ratham - āropya — taking onto His chariot
      Verb-phrase: making her mount the chariot. He does not merely hear about Kālindī — He puts her on His own conveyance. Gauḍīya: when the bhakta is ready, Bhagavān provides the vehicle. She does not walk to Hastināpura; she rides.
    • dharma - rājam — to Dharma-rāja (Yudhiṣṭhira)
      Compound dharma + rāja. Kṛṣṇa returns to the king of dharma before going further — He will not transport a future bride without informing the elder of the household. Gauḍīya: rasa never bypasses dharma.
    [Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued:] Arjuna repeated all this to Lord Vāsudeva, who was already aware of it. The Lord then took Kālindī onto His chariot and went back to see King Yudhiṣṭhira.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued:] Arjuna repeated all this to Lord Vāsudeva, who was already aware of it. The Lord then took Kālindī onto His chariot and went back to see King Yudhiṣṭhira.
    Commentary

    "I am that beautiful Visnu! Recognize me from the descriptions of Visnu taught by your father, and by your own emotions arising in your pure heart." After saying this he let her onto the chariot, for there is no mention that he put her to the chariot. Krsna already knew (tad vidvan) what Arjuna was coming to explain to him.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa already knew her intentions (tad-vidvān). He went to Yudhiṣṭhira, who knew everything (rājam) because of his knowledge of dharma.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Arjuna repeated what she said. How? He had conquered māyā (gudākeśaḥ). He did it out of affection for his cousin, the son of Vasudeva. But Kṛṣṇa already knew. She is fully dedicated to me only. Thus it is not proper to give her to Arjuna. It is also not suitable to ignore the criticism of being touched by lust by accepting many women in marriage. I will instruct all people by first sending Arjuna. He considered this first before sending Arjuna. Knowing dharma, the king will understand everything (dharma-rājam).

    • sandiṣṭaḥ — requested
      From sam + √diś — instructed. Kṛṣṇa is the one Viśvakarmā receives orders from. Gauḍīya: even the celestial architect builds at Bhagavān's signal; civilizational works begin in His mind.
    • viśvakarmaṇā — by Viśvakarmā
      The celestial architect. Builder of Indra's palace, Laṅkā, Dvārakā, and Indraprastha. The same hands that built Rāvaṇa's city now build the city of dharma — Gauḍīyas: the artisan is one; the patron determines the rasa.
    • adbhutam — amazing
      Wonder-causing. Adbhuta is one of the nine rasas of literary tradition. The Bhāgavatam tags Indraprastha with this rasa-word — the city is itself a poem in stone.
    • pārthānām — for the sons of Pṛthā
      Plural genitive. The city is built for the brothers as a group — not for Yudhiṣṭhira alone. Gauḍīya: bhakti is given to households, not just individuals; the gift sustains a kinship.
    [Describing a previous incident, Śukadeva Gosvāmī said:] Upon the request of the Pāṇḍavas, Lord Kṛṣṇa had Viśvakarmā build them a most wonderful and amazing city.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī mentions that this city was constructed before the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest and hence before the Lord found His bride Kālindī.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Describing a previous incident, Śukadeva Gosvāmī said:]Upon the request of the Pāṇḍavas, Lord Kṛṣṇa had Viśvakarmā build them a most wonderful and amazing city.
    Commentary

    The order of events is : first, the building of the city, then the burning of the Khandhava forest, then the building of the assembly hall and then gaining Kalindi as his wife. Being requested by the Pandavas, he had Visvakarma build a city.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord acted for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas in another way. This is a previous incident, explained in four verses. The order of events is this. The city was built. Then the Khāṇḍava forest was burned. Then Arjuna took the assembly hall from that place. Finally Kṛṣṇa accepted Kālindī. The word eva indicates that Kṛṣṇa was under the control of Pāṇḍavas. At their request alone, he had the city built. The city was most astonishing because it was variegated (vicitram), endowed with multifarious splendors from the fourteen worlds.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord acted for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas in another way. This is a previous incident, explained in four verses. Only because of the Pāṇdavas request (eva) he who is directly svayam bhgvavān (kṛṣṇaḥ) had the city built by Viśvakarmā. It was most astonishing, indescribable or beyond all human capacity because it was endowed with the various beauties of the fourteen worlds. It was greater than Indra’s city.

    Important Words
    • svānām — for His own (devotees)
      Genitive plural of sva — His own. The Bhāgavatam never tires of this word: He acts for His own. Gauḍīya: the bhakta becomes Kṛṣṇa's sva — His possession — and that ownership flips into His service of the owned.
    • priya - cikīrṣayā — desiring to please (His devotees)
      Compound priya (dear) + cikīrṣā (desire to do). Kṛṣṇa acts not from need but from the desire to please those dear to Him. Gauḍīya: His agency is rasa-driven; bhakti is the cause of His action.
    • sārathiḥ — charioteer
      The Supreme Lord as charioteer. Gauḍīya tradition holds sārathi-līlā among the most cherished sakhya episodes — Bhagavān reducing Himself to the box of the chariot for His friend's task. The Gītā's tableau begins here.
    • khāṇḍavam — the Khāṇḍava (forest)
      The forest given to Agni — a deep doctrinal moment: Agni's hunger and Arjuna's prowess meet by Kṛṣṇa's design. Gauḍīyas note: the burning is not destruction but offering. Agni eats what Kṛṣṇa has authorised him to eat.
    The Supreme Lord stayed in that city for some time to please His devotees. On one occasion, Śrī Kṛṣṇa wanted to give the Khāṇḍava forest as a gift to Agni, and so the Lord became Arjuna’s charioteer.
    Purport

    Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī explains the sequence of events that occurred during Lord Kṛṣṇa’s stay with the Pāṇḍavas. He states that first the Khāṇḍava forest was burned, then Kālindī was found, then the city was constructed, and then the assembly hall was presented to the Pāṇḍavas.

    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya

    The Supreme Lord stayed in that city for some time to please His devotees. On one occasion, Śrī Kṛṣṇa wanted to give the Khāṇḍava forest as a gift to Agni, and so the Lord became Arjuna's charioteer.
    Commentary

    Krsna became Arjuna's chariot driver so that Arjuna would get his weapons. Khandhava was a forest of Indra.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord stayed there a long time happily (ni—vāsan). He became Arjuna’s charioteer so Arjuna could gain his bow. This was a side effect of giving the forest to Agni.

    Analogy

    A king sometimes lets his cook offer the rice to fire; sometimes He drives a friend's chariot Himself. Kṛṣṇa becoming Arjuna's sārathi for the Khāṇḍava burning is sakhya in its boldest stroke — Bhagavān as charioteer of His friend.

    Stories
    Sārathi at Kurukṣetra

    The image foreshadowed here — Kṛṣṇa as Arjuna's charioteer — will become the central tableau of the Bhagavad-gītā (BG 1.20 onward). Pārtha-sārathi.

    Gauḍīya reading: in sakhya, the Lord accepts the position of subordinate. Driver, not warrior. The same friend who later sings the Gītā here drives the chariot for the burning of Khāṇḍava. The rasa is consistent; only the audience changes.

    Important Words
    • agniḥ — Lord Agni
      The god of fire. In Vedic theology, Agni is hotṛ — the priest who carries offerings to the gods. Here he is the recipient; the roles flip because Kṛṣṇa has redrawn the scene. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān reorders even cosmic functions.
    • akṣayau - tūṇau — inexhaustible quivers
      Plural — two quivers that never empty. The same word akṣaya from verse 13–14. Gauḍīya: instruments touched by Kṛṣṇa's līlā become akṣaya; depletion is a feature of māyā alone.
    • varma — armor
      Protective gear. Agni's gift answers what the warrior body needs. Gauḍīyas read armor here as the visible symbol of Kṛṣṇa's protection — the bhakta wrapped in invulnerability when Bhagavān is satisfied.
    • śvetān — white
      White horses — a Vedic mark of supreme purity (cf. Aśvamedha). Arjuna's chariot now carries the colours of yajña itself, gift of the very fire he satisfied.
    Being pleased, O King, Lord Agni presented Arjuna with a bow, a set of white horses, a chariot, a pair of inexhaustible quivers, and armor that no fighter could pierce with weapons.

    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Being pleased, O King, Lord Agni presented Arjuna with a bow, a set of white horses, a chariot, a pair of inexhaustible quivers, and armor that no fighter could pierce with weapons.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Agni also gave Kṛṣṇa the cakra. Because that is well known for other sources, it is not mentioned here. Satisfied with devouring the forest, Agni gave Arjuna the bow. O king! Śukadeva expresses his joy that Parīkṣit’s grandfather had obtained the bow.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Having devoured the Khāṇdava forest (saḥ) Agni gave to Arjuna a white chariot along with white horses.. The chariot was white since it was decorated with many pearl garlands and the white flag of Hanumān. O king! Śukadeva shouts in joy at the attainments of Parīkṣit’s grandfather.

    When fire is properly served, fire returns gifts that fire alone can give — and the gifts come to the one whose strength fed it. Agni's tribute to Arjuna is rasa keeping its accounts straight.

    Important Words
    • mayaḥ — the demon named Maya
      Maya Dānava — the asura architect, counterpart to Viśvakarmā. His name and the word māyā are root-cousins; his constructions specialize in optical reversal. Gauḍīya: he is rescued by Arjuna's mercy, and his gift carries the rescuer's friendship and the rescued's nature both.
    • mocitaḥ — delivered
      Past participle of √muc — released. Arjuna releases Maya from Agni's reach. Gauḍīya: even a sakhā-warrior's act of mercy is folded into Kṛṣṇa's larger līlā — that mercy fathers the dice-game which fathers the war.
    • sakhye — to his friend, Arjuna
      Dative of sakhi. Maya offers the sabhā to his sakhā Arjuna — the word sakhya threads through this chapter. Gauḍīya: every relation in the Pāṇḍava world is rasa-tinted; even an asura learns to call a Pāṇḍava 'friend'.
    • bhramaḥ — confusion
      From √bhram — to wander. The same root as bhrānti (verse 10). The Bhāgavatam plants this word in the verse to flag what Duryodhana will become: not a man with weapons but a man with bhrama, lost in māyā.
    When the demon Maya was saved from the fire by his friend Arjuna, Maya presented him with an assembly hall, in which Duryodhana would later mistake water for a solid floor.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the demon Maya was saved from the fire by his friend Arjuna, Maya presented him with an assembly hall, in which Duryodhana would later mistake water for a solid floor.
    Commentary

    Maya gave the assembly hall to Arjuna, his friend who saved him from the fire (sakha). Within that assembly hall Duryodhana later became bewildered.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Maya was saved from the fire by the Lord.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord saved the demon, and the demon gave the friend of Arjuna or the friend of the Lord the hall. Or he gave the hall out of friendship with the Pāṇḍavas. This was different from the Sudharma hall of Dvārakā. It is further described: Duryodhana would mistake water for land.

    Concepts
    MayaJiva
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A craftsman saved from fire repays his rescuer with a craftsman's gift — a house that itself plays tricks on those who do not see truly. Maya's sabhā is asura-māyā's most refined product, and it will undo Duryodhana before any weapon does.

    Stories
    Duryodhana's water-floor

    Mahābhārata, Sabhā-parva, records that Duryodhana, visiting the assembly hall Maya built, mistook crystal floor for water and water for floor — fell into the water, was laughed at by Draupadī (or so he heard), and conceived the rage that would burn into the dice game.

    Gauḍīyas: the sabhā built by an asura's hand carried asura-māyā in its grain. Maya's gift was real generosity, but it could not help showing the asura mind to itself. The seed of the war is in this house.

    Important Words
    • samanujñātaḥ — given leave
      From sam + anu + √jñā — fully consented. Kṛṣṇa does not slip away; He takes formal permission. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān's departure is choreographed with His devotees, not imposed on them.
    • su - hṛdbhiḥ — by His well-wishers
      Compound su (good) + hṛd (heart). The Pāṇḍavas as suhṛts — the same word from verse 10 (Kṛṣṇa as suhṛt of all). Now the bhaktas reciprocate the bhāva. Gauḍīya: suhṛd-bhāva is mutual in mature relation.
    • anumoditaḥ — allowed
      From anu + √mud — joyfully permitted. Not grudging consent but glad consent. Gauḍīya: rasa requires that even partings be accompanied by mutual ānanda; sorrow at separation is paradoxically a higher form of joy.
    • dvārakām — to Dvārakā
      The city Kṛṣṇa Himself had built (cf. Mausala-parva and SB 10.50). Returning to Dvārakā readies the stage for the next marriage. Gauḍīya: Dvārakā is Bhagavān's householder-līlā capital; every new wife enters there.
    Then Lord Kṛṣṇa, given leave by Arjuna and other well-wishing relatives and friends, returned to Dvārakā with Sātyaki and the rest of His entourage.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Then Lord Kṛṣṇa, given leave by Arjuna and other well-wishing relatives and friends, returned to Dvārakā with Sātyaki and the rest of His entourage.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After speaking previous events, Śukadeva returns to the events after receiving Kālindī. Receiving definite permission (sam—anujṣātaḥ) from Yudhiṣṭhira (tena), after repeatedly asking. He did not go previously because he understood affectionate Yudhiṣṭhira’s unwillingness to let him leave. Arjuna and others (suhrḍbhiḥ) also permitted this. The word saḥ (he) also indicates that Kṛṣṇa went with Kālindī, whom he would marry.

    Important Words
    • upayeme — He married
      From upa + √yam — to take (in marriage). The technical Sanskrit verb for marriage. This word will repeat at verse 56 (Bhadrām upayeme), threading the chapter's five marriages with one root.
    • kālindīm — Kālindī
      She who waited in the Yamunā now becomes a queen of Dvārakā. Gauḍīyas note: her name preserves her Vraja-affiliation even in her new station — she carries the river into the marriage.
    • ṛkṣe — lunar asterism
      A nakṣatra — one of the 27 lunar stations. The Bhāgavatam lists astrological propriety carefully; Vaiṣṇava marriage honours muhūrta-śāstra. Gauḍīya: bhakti includes time, not just bhāva.
    • parama - maṅgalaḥ — supremely auspicious
      Compound parama + maṅgala. Kṛṣṇa Himself is maṅgala — the auspiciousness an auspicious day points toward. Gauḍīya: He is not married on an auspicious day; the day becomes auspicious because He marries on it.
    The supremely auspicious Lord then married Kālindī on a day when the season, the lunar asterism and the configurations of the sun and other heavenly bodies were all propitious. In this way He brought the greatest pleasure to His devotees.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The supremely auspicious Lord then married Kālindī on a day when the season, the lunar asterism and the configurations of the sun and other heavenly bodies were all propitious. In this way He brought the greatest pleasure to His devotees.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The season and constellation were suitable for marriage (supuṇya) and the sun was strong by season (ūrjite), and moon and benefic planets were situated in beneficial constellations. Of course by his very nature Kṛṣṇa was most auspicious (parama-maṅgalaḥ). He chose this time only to teach the people. Or, by his own influence he made everything auspicious.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After coming to Dvārakā (atha) he married Kālindī. Or atha simply indicates auspiciousness. Thus auspiciousness is indicated. The constellations of the season were strong (ūrjite). Naturally they were auspicious but to teach the people, uttarāyaṇa, Māgha month etc. should be chosen. After the four months of monsoon during Mārgaśīrṣa month, after Kṛṣṇa returned to Dvārakā, with all its wealth, the marriage was performed, because Kṛṣṇa himself was most auspicious (parama-maṅgalaḥ). By his influence everything became auspicious. He gave bliss to Vasudeva and other relatives. He always gave bliss, but now, with the marriage to Kālindī he gave especially (vitanvan) the highest bliss.

    Important Words
    • duryodhana - vaśa - anugau — subservient to Duryodhana
      Compound — under Duryodhana's control. Politics has already chosen sides; Mitravindā's brothers are not free to discern. Gauḍīya: when worldly faction speaks louder than family bhāva, the sister must be rescued.
    • svayamvare — in the ceremony of choosing her own husband
      From sva (own) + vara (choice). The svayaṁvara is in principle the woman's free choice — and yet her brothers have forbidden the choice she would make. The Bhāgavatam exposes the contradiction in one word.
    • saktām — attached
      Past participle of √sañj — attached. The same root as saṅga (verse 3). Mitravindā's heart is already saṅga-saktā to Kṛṣṇa; the brothers are forbidding what is already real.
    • bhaginīm — sister
      From bhāga — share. A sister is one who shares the parental wealth. Bhāgavatam quietly stresses kinship — the brothers fail their share of sisterly love; Kṛṣṇa, the cousin, will keep it.
    Vindya and Anuvindya, who shared the throne of Avantī, were followers of Duryodhana’s. When the time came for their sister [Mitravindā] to select her husband in the svayaṁvara ceremony, they forbade her to choose Kṛṣṇa, although she was attracted to Him.
    Purport

    The feelings of enmity between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas were so strong that Mitravindā’s brothers, out of friendship for Duryodhana, forbade the young maiden to accept Kṛṣṇa as her husband.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Vindya and Anuvindya, who shared the throne of Avantī, were followers of Duryodhana's. When the time came for their sister [Mitravindā] to select her husband in the svayaṁvara ceremony, they forbade her to choose Kṛṣṇa, although she was attracted to Him.
    Commentary

    Two verse describe Krsna’s marriage to Mitravinda, his fifth wife. Vinda and Anuvinda were two kings of Avanti.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though it was a matter of choice, the brothers prevented their sister who was attracted to Kṛṣṇa from marrying him.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though it was a matter of choice (svyaṁvare), the brothers prevented their sister who was attracted to Kṛṣṇa from marrying him. Or she was attracted to Kṛṣṇa, who stole her (svayaṁvare). Or the brothers forbade her to choose by herself (svayaṁ vare). They were followers of Duryodhana. They followed his desire. Kṛṣṇa stole her though she was the daughter of his aunt because his heart was attracted by the prema of his dear devotee (kṛṣṇe).

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Sometimes a sister's brothers obstruct her from the choice her heart has already made — and the very obstruction reveals where her heart lives. Mitravindā's silence under her brothers' veto is louder than any speech.

    Stories
    Rukmiṇī's letter

    In SB 10.52, Rukmiṇī's brother Rukmī also forbade her to marry Kṛṣṇa, planning her marriage to Śiśupāla. Rukmiṇī wrote her famous letter — and Kṛṣṇa came in person to abduct her at the temple of Ambikā.

    Mitravindā's situation reprises that grammar exactly: a sister attached to Kṛṣṇa, brothers in Duryodhana's faction obstructing, and Bhagavān stepping in to take her openly. Gauḍīya: a sister's bhakti has higher authority than a brother's politics.

    Important Words
    • rājādhidevyāḥ — of Queen Rājādhidevī
      Mitravindā's mother — and Kṛṣṇa's paternal aunt (his father Vasudeva's sister). Gauḍīya: the kinship is doctrinally important. Kṛṣṇa takes His own cousin; this is not a stranger's marriage but a family return.
    • pitṛ - svasuḥ — of His father's sister
      Compound pitṛ (father) + svasṛ (sister). Mitravindā is Kṛṣṇa's paternal aunt's daughter — His pitṛ-svasuḥ-tanayā. Marrying a paternal aunt's daughter is, in many regions of India, a recognized cousin-marriage.
    • prasahya — forcibly
      From pra + √sah — by overpowering. The Bhāgavatam does not soften the word: He took her by force. Gauḍīya: kṣatriya-dharma allows rākṣasa-vivāha (taking the bride by valour) when conventional means are blocked — and Bhagavān models it.
    • prapaśyatām — while watching
      Genitive plural of present participle — of those watching. The kings are reduced to onlookers. Gauḍīya: when Bhagavān acts, those who would oppose Him are downgraded to spectators in their own assembly.
    My dear King, Lord Kṛṣṇa forcibly took away Princess Mitravindā, the daughter of His aunt Rājādhidevī, before the eyes of the rival kings.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My dear King, Lord Kṛṣṇa forcibly took away Princess Mitravindā, the daughter of His aunt Rājādhidevī, before the eyes of the rival kings.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Marriage between relatives (in this case cousins) was allowed in the Yadu dynasty. Because Mitravindā was attracted to Kṛṣṇa (one who attracts), Kṛṣṇa responded appropriately by accepting her. Since she came from Śibi province, she was called Śaibyā. Later Draupadī addresses her in this way during the journey to Kurukṣetra. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains that in his commentary on that episode.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O king! Śukadeva calls out in joy at the mercy given to the Lord’s devotee. Or Kṛṣṇa was shining (rājan). He stole her while the kings watched in bliss, or though they saw it, he disregarded them. Since she came from Śibi province, she was called Śaibyā. Later Draupadī addresses her in this way during the journey to Kurukṣetra. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains that in his commentary on that episode.

    Important Words
    • nagnajit — Nagnajit
      King of Kośala (the same kingdom over which Rāma once reigned). His name — 'conqueror of the naked / shameless' — suggests dharma's victor. Gauḍīya: this marriage takes Kṛṣṇa into Rāma's old kingdom; the Bhāgavatam threads avatāric continuity.
    • kauśalyaḥ — ruler of Kośala (Ayodhyā)
      Of Kośala — the kingdom of Rāmacandra. Gauḍīyas: by marrying the Kośala princess, Kṛṣṇa as the same Bhagavān who was Rāma quietly returns to His old capital, now in a new bridegroom-form.
    • ati - dhārmikaḥ — very pious
      Compound ati (very) + dhārmika (righteous). Nagnajit's piety is the verse's first claim about him. Gauḍīya: dharma-niṣṭha households produce kṛṣṇa-niṣṭha daughters.
    • satyā — Satyā
      Her primary name — 'the true one'. Truth is her substance, not merely her label. Gauḍīya: a wife of Kṛṣṇa is named for the metaphysical category He embodies (kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam — He is the satyam-param).
    • nāgnajitī — Nāgnajitī
      Patronymic — daughter of Nagnajit. The Bhāgavatam stacks her two names: she is the truth and the daughter of the king of dharma. Naming is doctrinal economy.
    O King, Nagnajit, the very pious King of Kośala, had a lovely daughter named Satyā, or Nāgnajitī.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O King, Nagnajit, the very pious King of Kauśalya, had a lovely daughter named Satyā, or Nāgnajitī.
    Commentary

    The sixth marriage is described. Nagnajit was the king of Ayodhya. His daughter was called Satya.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nagnajit was dedicated to bhagavat-dharma (atidhārmikaḥ). Nagnajit means he who conquers even the naked Jains. O king! You know the beauty and good conduct of princesses! Why do I have to describe it?

    Important Words
    • sapta — seven
      The number to remember through the rest of the episode. Seven bulls; seven Kṛṣṇas (verse 45). Gauḍīya: when Bhagavān must answer a sevenfold problem He generates a sevenfold solution; the asymmetry vanishes.
    • go - vṛṣān — bulls
      Compound go (cow) + vṛṣa (bull). Tīrtha-vṛṣa or simply vṛṣa — bulls. Gauḍīya note: Kṛṣṇa is gopāla, master of cows; the bulls of His future father-in-law are kin to His own herd. Subduing them is a family gesture.
    • durdharṣān — unbreakable
      From dur (difficult) + √dharṣ — hard to overpower. The bulls are the visible image of every barrier worldly suitors face. Gauḍīya: difficulty is reserved by Bhagavān for His own showcase.
    • vīrya - gandha - asahān — unable to bear the scent of valour
      Compound — they cannot tolerate the smell of warriors. A near-impossible condition: even a brave smell defeats them. Gauḍīya: the test is rigged against ordinary heroism. Only Bhagavān's līlā-strength will pass.
    The kings who came as suitors were not allowed to marry her unless they could subdue seven sharp-horned bulls. These bulls were extremely vicious and uncontrollable, and they could not tolerate even the smell of warriors.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The kings who came as suitors were not allowed to marry her unless they could subdue seven sharp-horned bulls. These bulls were extremely vicious and uncontrollable, and they could not tolerate even the smell of warriors.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Thought the father wanted to give his daughter to the Lord, because of fear of rivals like Jarāsandha, he devised a method for her marriage. Go-vṛṣāṇ simply means bulls using two words, or the best (vṛṣān) bulls (go), or the most uncontrollable bulls (vṛṣān) among all the cattle (go). Without tying up (ajitvā) the bulls they could not marry her. The bulls were violent (khalān), having the nature of demons. In the Second Canto these bulls are counted among the demons. (SB 2.7.34) It is stated there that after being killed, by the power of the Lord’s touch, they attained liberation.

    A bride-condition that no king has met is not a barrier but an invitation — held in reserve for the one who will not merely meet it but multiply Himself to meet it. The seven bulls are waiting for the seven Kṛṣṇas.

    Important Words
    • vṛṣa - jit — by him who conquers the bulls
      Compound vṛṣa (bull) + jit (conqueror). The man-who-can-do-it is named in advance. Gauḍīya: this kind of compound — defining the hero by the deed yet to be done — is the Bhāgavatam telling the reader Bhagavān is already that hero before He even arrives.
    • bhagavān — the Supreme Lord
      The Bhāgavatam's preferred title throughout. The wedding-test does not reduce Bhagavān; the title remains in place even as He performs an ostensibly worldly feat. Gauḍīya: the same Bhagavān who lifts Govardhana subdues seven bulls — same agent, different scale.
    • sātvatām - patiḥ — Lord of the Sātvatas
      Compound — the Sātvatas are the Yadu clan. Kṛṣṇa moves not just as svayaṁ-bhagavān but as the head of His family. Gauḍīya: marriage is a clan event; Bhagavān comes representing the Yadu-vaṁśa, not as an individual.
    • sainyena - mahatā - vṛtaḥ — accompanied by a great army
      Phrase — surrounded by a vast army. The military entourage marks the courtship's seriousness. Gauḍīya: rasa does not exclude pomp; kṣatriya-vivāha is a state visit, not a private errand.
    When the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the master of the Vaiṣṇavas, heard of the princess who was to be won by the conqueror of the bulls, He went to the capital of Kauśalya with a large army.

    When the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the master of the Vaiṣṇavas, heard of the princess who was to be won by the conqueror of the bulls, He went to the capital of Kauśalya with a large army.
    Commentary

    No one could marry her without taming the seven bulls.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord, endowed with all powers (bhagavān), the protector of the devotees (sātvatāṁ patiḥ), understanding all the kings would be going there, went there, surrounded by a huge army.

    Important Words
    • kośala - patiḥ — the lord of Kośala
      Compound — the same title once held by Daśaratha. Gauḍīya undertone: the king of Kośala once welcomed Rāma as his eldest son; now another Kośala-king welcomes the same Bhagavān as a son-in-law. Avatāric memory.
    • pratyutthāna — by standing up
      From prati + ud + √sthā — rising in greeting. A specific śāstric form of honour. The king rises from his throne, the highest gesture a host can offer. Gauḍīya: pratyutthāna is the bodily form of accepting that the guest outranks the seat.
    • guruṇā — great
      Heavy — substantial gifts. Hospitality measured by weight, not flourish. Gauḍīyas: rasa requires substance; ornamentation without substance is hollow.
    • pratinanditaḥ — (Lord Kṛṣṇa) greeted respectfully in return
      From prati + nand — to gladden in return. The greeting is reciprocal; Kṛṣṇa does not merely receive worship, He greets the host. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān honours dharma's exchanges; reciprocity is rasa.
    The King of Kośala, pleased to see Lord Kṛṣṇa, worshiped Him by rising from his throne and offering Him a seat of honor and substantial gifts. Lord Kṛṣṇa also greeted the King respectfully.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The King of Kośala, pleased to see Lord Kṛṣṇa, worshiped Him by rising from his throne and offering Him a seat of honor and substantial gifts. Lord Kṛṣṇa also greeted the King respectfully.
    Commentary

    The king worshipped Krsna and greeted him. Krsna also worshipped him.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The king, with a pretext for giving Kṛṣṇa his daughter, was pleased. He worshipped him by offering a seat according to custom and then worshipped him according to the scriptures, with suitable articles. The word ādibhiḥ indicates that he washed his feet, fanned him and did other services.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The king was famous for following dharma (saḥ) or wanted to give his daughter to Kṛṣṇa. Ādibhiḥ indicates giving arghya, pādya and other items. He worshipped him with the best (gurunā) items, such as ornaments. This could also include arghya etc. but to stress the importance they are mentioned separately or they are mentioned separately because of the particular method he used in offering separately.

    Important Words
    • abhimatam — agreeable
      From abhi + √man — set the mind upon. Kṛṣṇa is the one her mind has settled on. Gauḍīya: bhāva-bhakti's mark is that the mind has already chosen before any external test is run.
    • cakame — she desired
      From √kam — to desire. The same root as kāma. Yet here it is not material kāma but bhakta-rūpā-kāma — the wish for the right Lord. Gauḍīya: not all desire is bondage; rightly-directed kāma is bhakti's seed.
    • ramā - patim — the Lord of Goddess Rāma (Lakṣmī)
      Compound — Lakṣmī's husband. Satyā's prayer recognises the cosmic identity: He is Lakṣmī's already; she begs to be His too. Gauḍīya: any bride of Kṛṣṇa knows Lakṣmī precedes her — and is content.
    • analaḥ — the (sacred) fire
      Agni. Satyā prays through the fire because Agni is the witness of Vedic vows. Gauḍīya: the same fire that burned Khāṇḍava (verse 25) and gave Arjuna his bow (verse 26) now is invoked as a marriage-witness. Bhagavān's līlās link by their elements.
    • vrataḥ — vow
      From √vṛ — to choose. The same root as vṛṇe (verse 21). Satyā's silent vow joins Kālindī's spoken one — both women's tapas-vows are the bhakti-grammar of this chapter.
    When the King’s daughter saw that most agreeable suitor arrive, she immediately desired to have Him, the Lord of Goddess Rāma. She prayed, “May He become my husband. If I have kept my vows, may the sacred fire bring about the fulfillment of my hopes.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the King's daughter saw that most agreeable suitor arrive, she immediately desired to have Him, the Lord of Goddess Rāma. She prayed, "May He become my husband. If I have kept my vows, may the sacred fire bring about the fulfillment of my hopes.
    Commentary

    She saw Krsna through the lattice windows from the watch tower.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The scene in the assembly was described. The scene when Kṛṣṇa was brought into the inner area with his relatives is described. She saw him from lattice holes in the roof pavilion. She saw the groom whom she had long desired and was the choice of all people (abhimatam), since he was the husband even of Rukmiṇī, the perfect Lakṣmī (ramā-patim). This means he was her eternal husband, endowed with the best qualities. She did not feel sorrow at being a co-wife. He went as far as was befitting a suitor (sam--āgatam) within the palace. Seeing him directly (vi-lokya), she became agitated with special emotions and made her vow (cakame). She was the king’s daughter (narendra-kanyāḥ), unable to tolerate agitation because of her tenderness. Her vow is described. May the fire, whom I have long worshipped as my deity, make my desires come true. Doubting the completeness of her worship, in a mood of longing, she then says “May the fire fulfill my desire, if the rules for worship were followed with attention.” Another version has āśiṣo ‘malaḥ (pure desire). In that case the meaning is “May he be mine. May this husband make the pure desire come true, if I have followed the rules with attention.”

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She long cherished (abhimatam) Kṛṣṇa since he was the lord of Lakṣmī or he was approved by all (abhimatam) by form and qualities or as the husband of Rukmiṇī (ramā-patim). Seeing him directly coming with his friends (samāgatam), she desired him because she was ornamented with all good form and qualities. What did she desire? May the fire, long worshipped by me, make my desires (āśiṣaḥ) true if my vow was performed according to rules, or if the rules of worship were followed with care. Plural of desires (āśiṣaḥ) is used to show respect.

    Analogy

    When the right suitor walks into the courtyard, the bride's body knows before her mind does — she does not survey; she recognizes. Satyā's quiet prayer to the sacred fire is recognition asking to be made factual.

    Stories
    Sāvitrī's choice of Satyavān

    When Sāvitrī, daughter of King Aśvapati, was sent to choose her own husband (Mahābhārata, Vana-parva), she returned saying she had chosen Satyavān — though she knew his life was short. Her choice was rooted in seeing.

    Satyā's seeing is the same gesture: when bhakti has matured into recognition, the choice is single. Gauḍīyas: a bhakta does not deliberate between Kṛṣṇa and others; she simply sees.

    Important Words
    • paṅkaja — lotuslike
      From paṅka (mud) + ja (born). The lotus rises clean from mud — Kṛṣṇa's feet are paṅkaja, even though He walks through worlds full of mud, untouched. Gauḍīya: the lotus is the universal sign for transcendence-within-immanence.
    • rajaḥ — the dust
      Pāda-dhūli — foot-dust. The traditional Gauḍīya object of supreme veneration; pādārpaṇa is the lowest and highest gift. Even Lakṣmī wears His foot-dust on her head. Gauḍīya: vraja-raja, the dust of Vṛndāvana, is itself worshipped for this reason.
    • līlā - tanuḥ — pastime form
      Compound līlā (play) + tanu (body). Bhagavān's avatāras are līlā-tanus, descended for sport — not for need. Gauḍīya: each incarnation is rasa's clothing for a moment; Kṛṣṇa as svayaṁ-bhagavān is the wearer.
    • setu — the codes of religion
      Literally — dyke, bridge. The dharma-setu is what holds the cosmic order from being washed away. Kṛṣṇa descends kāle kāle — age by age — to repair the setu. Gauḍīya echo of BG 4.7-8.
    “Goddess Lakṣmī, Lord Brahma, Lord Śiva and the rulers of the various planets place the dust of His lotus feet on their heads, and to protect the codes of religion, which He has created, He assumes pastime incarnations at various times. How may that Supreme Personality of Godhead become pleased with me?”
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    "Goddess Lakṣmī, Lord Brahma, Lord Śiva and the rulers of the various planets place the dust of His lotus feet on their heads, and to protect the codes of religion, which He has created, He assumes pastime incarnations at various times. How may that Supreme Personality of Godhead become pleased with me?"
    Commentary

    "How can I please that person who appears in the world when there is necessity of protecting the laws of religion made by himself, and who is now present here?"

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She lists great personalities from the greater to the lesser—Lakṣmī, Brahmā, Śiva and the rulers of planets, in order to show her own insignificance. Śiva is considered less than Brahmā because as Brahmā’s son he acts as his student and Brahmā was the direct utilizer of the eighteen syllable Kṛṣṇa mantra. He has accepted (adadhat, but should be adadhāt) various forms for pastimes, with a desire to protect the dharma he has created. This indicates that Kṛṣṇa is the avatārī, the source of the avatāras. Another version has parīpsayeśa instead of parīpsayā yaḥ. By what cause or what sādhana of a low person like me will Kṛṣṇa (saḥ), famous as Svayam bhagavān, be satisfied? I think there is no method at all.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “I am satisfied by bhakti.” Brahmā, who arose from the lotus in the Lord’s navel and who is thus his son, holds only one particle of his foot dust on his head. Śiva is considered secondary (sa-giriśaḥ) because Śiva appeared from Brahmā, and holds the dust by Brahmā’s order. Indra and others are also secondary. Śrī, first in the list, is the best. Śrī being closest to the Lord is mentioned first. Brahmā has the Lord’s affection, being his son. Then Śiva has the Lord’s affection. And then the devatās such as Indra have his affection. By his mercy, Indra and others carry the foot dust. Or Śiva (giriśaḥ), having great powers (sa), is famous as the friend of the Lord. But even he, to attain the rarely attained Lord, holds the dust along with the devatās like Indra. They all worship the Lord. This made clear in Hari-vaṁśa, in describing the theft of the pārijāta tree. Śrī and the others show devotion to the Lord. So who am I? Even in his avatāra forms it is rare for them to hold his foot dust. In order to protect the laws he has made, he accepts forms having various pastimes (līlā-tanuḥ) at appropriate times. When you become absorbed in your pastimes, they cannot attract your attention. Or among the avatāras manifested by your mercy, someone may satisfy one of them by some bhakti. But it is not possible to satisfy you, the source of the avatāras. But I, trespassing my dharma, am not qualified with bhakti. How, by what method, will the Lord who manifests unlimited powers (bhagavān), be satisfied with me? The potential form of the verb expresses possibility (tuṣyet). He cannot be satisfied.

    If Lakṣmī herself wears the dust of His feet as her ornament, what is left for a mortal princess to offer? Satyā's question is the universal humility of every bhakta who realises her gift cannot match His worth.

    Stories
    Lakṣmī's penance on Vaikuṇṭha

    Tradition holds that Lakṣmī herself performed long austerities to dwell on Bhagavān's chest (cf. SB 8.8). The supreme Goddess of Fortune chose, of all places, His thoracic region — and never left.

    Gauḍīya reading: when even Lakṣmī's place was hard-won, the lesser woman's prayer is necessarily one of kārpaṇya — what could she offer that He does not already have? Yet Bhagavān's joy is not in receiving rare gifts but in receiving devotion.

    Important Words
    • nārāyaṇa — O Nārāyaṇa
      Nara (men) + ayana (resting place). Kṛṣṇa is here addressed by His Vaiṣṇava cosmic name — Nagnajit signals his doctrinal awareness from the first word. Gauḍīya: Nārāyaṇa is the form of Bhagavān worshipped in Vaikuṇṭha; the king's address is theologically informed.
    • ātma - ānandena — in Your own spiritual pleasure
      Compound ātma (self) + ānanda (bliss). Bhagavān is full in His own bliss (ātma-ratiḥ, BG 3.17). Gauḍīya: He needs nothing; whatever a devotee offers He accepts as rasa, not as supplement.
    • pūrṇasya — of the complete
      Genitive — to one who is full. Echo of the famous Upaniṣadic mantra (Īśa) — pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam. Gauḍīya: the fullness of Bhagavān is not abstract; it is the rasa-saturation of His own form.
    • karavāṇi - kim — what can I do
      First-person optative + 'what'. The bhakta's foundational question. The king sees the asymmetry honestly: I have nothing to give that is not already Yours. Gauḍīya: this is the right opening of a devotee before Bhagavān.
    King Nagnajit first worshiped the Lord properly and then addressed Him: “O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the universe, You are full in Your own spiritual pleasure. Therefore what can this insignificant person do for You?”
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    King Nagnajit first worshiped the Lord properly and then addressed Him: "O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the universe, You are full in Your own spiritual pleasure. Therefore what can this insignificant person do for You?"
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After Kṛṣṇa had been worshipped (arcitam punaḥ), the king spoke to him. O shelter of all jīvas (nārāyaṇa)! Therefore you are the master of all objects (jagat-pate). What can I, smaller than the smallest (alpakaḥ), do for you, full of your own bliss. He uses the possessive case (purṇasya) which is indirect, to indicate his reverence, though Kṛṣṇa is visible in front of him.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The king again worshipped the Lord, because of great affection or in order to speak to him. O shelter of all jīvas! O protector of the universe! We cannot protect the citizens by levying taxes etc. You depend on nothing else. Your experience bliss in yourself. You have happiness by your nature. Or O Nārāyaṇa! O supreme Lord! O protector of the universe, master of all things! You are full of your own happiness. First the king expressed the Lord who is visible and then invisible out of great respect. What can I do for you, being very small? I can do nothing.

    Important Words
    • hṛṣṭaḥ — pleased
      Past participle of √hṛṣ — gladdened. Bhagavān is satisfied with the king's address. Gauḍīya: the bhakta's correct opening sentence already pleases the Lord; the result of the meeting is secured in the first speech.
    • megha - gambhīrayā — deep as a cloud
      Compound megha (cloud) + gambhīra (deep). Kṛṣṇa's voice resembles thunder — a recurrent Bhāgavatam image. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān's voice is the syllabic form of the sky, formidable and life-giving at once.
    • vācā — in a voice
      Instrumental of vāc — speech. Bhagavān's vāc is the seed of the Veda. Whatever He says now will be śruti for the king. Gauḍīya: every word from Kṛṣṇa's mouth is svayaṁ-pramāṇa, self-evidencing.
    • kuru - nandana — O beloved descendant of Kuru
      Vocative — Śuka addresses Parīkṣit. The narrator does not let the listener forget he is being addressed; the kuru-nandana is being told the kuru-history as his own family story. Gauḍīya: the Bhāgavatam's pravacana is always relational.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: O beloved descendant of Kuru, the Supreme Lord was pleased, and after accepting a comfortable seat He smiled and addressed the King in a voice as deep as the rumbling of a cloud.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: O beloved descendant of Kuru, the Supreme Lord was pleased, and after accepting a comfortable seat He smiled and addressed the King in a voice as deep as the rumbling of a cloud.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The first line of the verse indicates the good fortune of the king, whom the Lord accepted as his devotee. The second line shows how his heart was stolen by the Lord’s sweetness and mercy. The Lord accepted a seat which was offered for a long time. He was joyful because of the great bhakti of his devotee who desired him. This is shown by his acceptance of the seat, since he sat down in it comfortably. Kṛṣṇa smiled because of his nature, but also because of attaining his desire, with a little embarrassment. Out of excitement Śukadeva calls to Parīkṣit, “O son of the Kurus!”

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Lord was endowed with unlimited qualities like affection for his devotee (bhagavān). He accepted a seat which was offered for a long time. He stood for some time because he was being praised, and then sat. He smiled out of his nature or to give mercy to the king. Or knowing the king’s arrangements and desires, he felt inner joy at the request of the daughter. Out of excitement Śukadeva calls to Parīkṣit, “O son of the Kurus!”

    Important Words
    • yācñā — begging
      From √yāc — to ask. Bhagavān names His own action as yācñā — begging. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān begs from His own devotees what is already His; the begging is His rasa-art, not His need.
    • vigarhitā — condemned
      Past participle of vi + √garh — censured. Kavayas (learned authorities) censure begging by a kṣatriya. Bhagavān acknowledges the censure even as He sets it aside. Gauḍīya: rasa sometimes overrides śāstra's surface; bhakti is the meta-rule.
    • sauhṛda - icchayā — desiring friendship
      Compound sauhṛda (friendship, well-wishing) + icchā (desire). The motive admitted openly: the Lord wants friendship with this household. Gauḍīya: His asking is not a transaction; it is the bid for sauhṛda.
    • śulka - dāḥ — bride-price givers
      Compound śulka (bride-price) + dā (giver). Kṛṣṇa declares He brings no bride-price — yet (as verse 45 will show) He pays the price the king set: subduing the bulls. The economic exchange is replaced by valour. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān pays in līlā, not coin.
    The Supreme Lord said: O ruler of men, learned authorities condemn begging for a person in the royal order who is executing his religious duties. Even so, desiring your friendship, I ask you for your daughter, though We offer no gifts in exchange.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supreme Lord said: O ruler of men, learned authorities condemn begging for a person in the royal order who is executing his religious duties. Even so, desiring your friendship, I ask you for your daughter, though We offer no gifts in exchange.
    Commentary

    "Even one who is an inferior kstariya should not ask from another. Tthough I am a superior ksatriya I am asking. I ask for your daughter without dowry."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I act in accordance human pastimes which give the bliss of prema to my devotees. Because of your prema, I transgress the rules that should be followed. Kṛṣṇa speaks with a skilful request worthy of a kṣatriya, while indicating the scriptural conclusion. He addresses the king respectable as a father-in-law in order to make his relationship with him strong. O king (narendra)! Begging for even a fallen kṣatriya is strongly condemned (vi--garhitāḥ) by the wise sages like Vyāsadeva, since stealing by force is praised. With a desire of establishing a happy relationship with you (tava sauhṛdecchayā), or with a desire that you have prema for me, I, a kṣatriya, ask for your daughter, without offering any gifts. This is a profound joke, since in speaking of dharma, Kṛṣṇa understood the price of the bride to be his tying of the bulls.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I will be satisfied by your giving your daughter. Begging by kṣatriyas is condemned by poets like Vyāsa and especially condemned (vi-garhitaḥ) for those following their own dharma. Stealing the girl in the svayaṁbara is praised for kṣatriyas. O king you know this (narendra)! For having a good relationship with you (tava sauhṛdecchayā), or desiring that you have prema for me, I do not give a gift for certain (hi) for respecting the family. He uses the plural (vayam) to indicate the Yadu dynasty, out of respect for being born among them or to indicate the huge family of Yadus. Otherwise others would think him insignificant.

    Analogy

    A king does not ordinarily beg — yet the supreme Lord begs from a small king, and the begging is itself the great gift. Friendship's economy turns gifts inside out: in giving you nothing material, He gives you everything.

    Important Words
    • abhyadhikaḥ — superior
      From abhi + adhika — greater than. There is no one greater than Kṛṣṇa as son-in-law. Gauḍīya: the comparison is closed by definition; svayaṁ-bhagavān admits no superior.
    • guṇa - eka - dhāmnaḥ — the exclusive abode of all transcendental qualities
      Compound guṇa (quality) + eka (sole) + dhāman (abode). All auspicious qualities reside in one place — in Kṛṣṇa. Gauḍīya: the doctrine of bhagavat-tattva — Bhagavān is the locus of all ṣaḍ-aiśvarya (six opulences).
    • anapāyinī — never leaving
      From an (not) + apa + √i — non-departing. Śrī (Lakṣmī) never leaves Kṛṣṇa's chest. Gauḍīya: the wife in the marriage will be one in a household where Lakṣmī herself permanently dwells. The princess gains a sister in Lakṣmī, not a rival.
    The King said: My Lord, who could be a better husband for my daughter than You, the exclusive abode of all transcendental qualities? On Your body the goddess of fortune herself resides, never leaving You for any reason.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The King said: My Lord, who could be a better husband for my daughter than You, the exclusive abode of all transcendental qualities? On Your body the goddess of fortune herself resides, never leaving You for any reason.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though Lakṣmī is the shelter of all qualities, you are the abode of good qualities (guṇaika-dhāmnaḥ). Since she is controlled by your qualities, she has all qualities.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O Lord whom all people request to attain. One should desire to attain you. Who else is there, with qualities greater than yours? There is no one. His form is described as the reason for attaining him. Lakṣmī, always very steady, resides on the chest of your form (aṅge) since you are the extraordinary abode of all qualities like truth and cleanliness.

    Important Words
    • samayaḥ — a stipulation
      From sam + √i — an agreement. The king's prior public commitment. Gauḍīya: dharma does not unmake earlier dharma even when Bhagavān is the new context; honour preserves the test, and Bhagavān will simply pass.
    • sātvata - ṛṣabha — O chief of the Sātvatas
      Compound sātvata + ṛṣabha (bull, chief). The king addresses Kṛṣṇa as ṛṣabha — bull — exactly in the verse before he will speak of the bulls Kṛṣṇa must subdue. Gauḍīya: the metaphor lands twice; the bull-chief versus the bulls.
    • vīrya - parīkṣā — test of prowess
      Compound vīrya (valour) + parīkṣā (test). The bride-test is martial — the suitor must show vīrya. Gauḍīya: the same Bhagavān whom yogīs cannot see is being asked to show vīrya for one bride. He consents.
    But to ascertain the proper husband for my daughter, O chief of the Sātvatas, we previously set a condition to test the prowess of her suitors.
    Purport

    According to Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī, the King’s actual purpose in setting up the test was to obtain Śrī Kṛṣṇa as his son-in-law, since only He could subdue the bulls. Without such a test it would have been difficult for Nagnajit to refuse the many apparently qualified princes and kings who came to ask for his daughter’s hand in marriage.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    But to ascertain the proper husband for my daughter, O chief of the Sātvatas, we previously set a condition to test the prowess of her suitors.
    Commentary

    The king answers Krsna's statement that he will give no dowry. "But I have made a rule to test the strength of the groom, if he wants to gain my daughter as his bride. Otherwise all the kings would ask for her and how could I agree to all of them. You, whose outstanding form and qualities are already known, are the most suitable to be the groom. I made the rule so that only you could take her."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I and my relatives have made a rule previously. With a desire to obtain for my daughter a qualified groom (kanyā-vara-parīpsayā), or because of the desire of the groom for my daughter, we have made a rule in order to test the courage and strength of the man. You should also follow our rule, O maintainter of the devotees.

    Important Words
    • durdāntāḥ — wild
      From dur + √dam — untameable. The standard Sanskrit adjective for what no taming has subdued. Gauḍīya: every durdānta thing in the world meets its damana in Kṛṣṇa; cf. Kāliya-damana, Aghāsura-damana.
    • duravagrahāḥ — unbreakable (resistant to restraint)
      From dur + ava + √grah — hard to hold. Even ropes will not bind them ordinarily. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān binds the unbindable just as Yaśodā fails and then succeeds with the dāmodara-rope (SB 10.9) — the chapter's verse 46 will echo bāla-līlā.
    • bhinna - gātrāḥ — broken-limbed
      Compound bhinna (broken) + gātra (limb). The bulls have broken many princes' bones. The verse counts the casualties so the reader knows the cost. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān's līlā does not minimise others' suffering; it transcends it.
    These seven wild bulls are impossible to tame, O hero. They have defeated many princes, breaking their limbs.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    These seven wild bulls are impossible to tame, O hero. They have defeated many princes, breaking their limbs.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Clearing himself and his people of fault, he then explains the rule. When Kṛṣṇa accepted, the king went to the bull pen and pointed with his finger. These (ete) are the seven bulls. They have broken the limbs of the princes and defeated them. By this he suggests that by this he had arranged for the defeat of the princes who were Kṛṣṇa’s enemies. O hero (vīra), by your strength you will control the bulls.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    These (ete) are the seven bulls. He indicates their presence by pointing with his finger. Because of them or by them, many princes have been defeated, because their limbs were broken. They were sons of kings—young and strong. O hero (vīra)! By your prowess you will tie them up, all by yourself. O joy of the Yadus! You should to this to give joy to the Yadus. O husband of Lakṣmī! I agree to this because you are the master of Lakṣmī.

    Important Words
    • yadu - nandana — O descendant of Yadu
      Compound yadu + nandana (joy). The king addresses Kṛṣṇa by His clan-name — placing the marriage in family register. Gauḍīya: nandana means delight; Kṛṣṇa is the delight of His family, even before becoming the delight of His bride.
    • śriyaḥ - pate — O Lord of Śrī
      Vocative compound — husband of Lakṣmī. The king names what Kṛṣṇa already is. Gauḍīya: the bride is being given to one who already has Lakṣmī; no rivalry can arise because the throne is fixed.
    • abhimataḥ — the appropriate bridegroom
      From abhi + √man — agreed-upon. Repeats verse 36's abhimatam — first the bride's mind found Him agreeable, now the father's. Both yes-es line up. Gauḍīya: bhakti's consent is layered; family yes and personal yes both.
    If You can subdue them, O descendant of Yadu, You will certainly be the appropriate bridegroom for my daughter, O Lord of Śrī.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    If You can subdue them, O descendant of Yadu, You will certainly be the appropriate bridegroom for my daughter, O Lord of Śrī.
    Commentary

    In this sentence yad means "if," or more correcly "because." "Because you control the seven bulls, you can marry my daughter." By addressing Krsna as the master of Laksmi, he declares that Krsna is her husband, since he can control the bulls. He had kept the bulls just to be killed by Krsna as they were inimical to him.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Yadi indicates certainty as in the following. Dhatse padaṁ tvam avitā yadi vighna-mūrddhni: because you are the direct protector of your devotee, he is able to step over the head of whatever obstacle the demigods place before him. (SB 11.4.10) You will certainly subdue the bulls. Or, since you will subdue the bulls, you will be the appropriate groom. You alone are suitable since others will not be able to do this because the bulls are strong and the bulls cannot harm you because of they are only bulls. In order to fulfill our desires and our promise, you should do this. You should also do this to give joy to the Yadus (yadu-nandana).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O joy of the Yadus! You should to this to give joy to the Yadus. O husband of Lakṣmī! I agree to this because you are the master of Lakṣmī. By subduing the bulls, you have permission to take my daughter. Or you are the appropriate groom since you are the husband of Rukmiṇī.

    Important Words
    • baddhvā - parikaram — tightening His clothing
      Verb-phrase: girding up. A homely, athletic gesture. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān prepares for the contest as a kṣatriya would — line by line. The līlā is in the details.
    • saptadhā — into seven (parts)
      Adverbial from sapta (seven) + dhā (manner). Sevenfold. Gauḍīya: Bhagavān's bahudhā (manifold) capability is exercised in exactly the number required. Plenitude is precise, not vague.
    • nyagṛhṇāt — He subdued
      Imperfect of ni + √grah — to take down, restrain. The same verbal field as nigṛhīta (verse 44 — subdued). Gauḍīya: each bull is grasped, individually, by His matching form. Bhagavān does not herd; He addresses each.
    • līlayā — easily (playfully)
      Instrumental of līlā — by sport. The whole feat is līlā — effortless, joyful. Gauḍīya: this is the foundational adverb of Bhāgavata theology; everything Bhagavān does, He does līlayā, never śrameṇa (with toil).
    Upon hearing these terms, the Lord tightened His clothing, expanded Himself into seven forms and easily subdued the bulls.
    Purport

    According to Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī, Lord Kṛṣṇa expanded Himself into seven forms not only to playfully defeat the seven bulls but also to show Princess Satya that she would not have to compete with His other queens, since He could enjoy with all of them simultaneously.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Upon hearing these terms, the Lord tightened His clothing, expanded Himself into seven forms and easily subdued the bulls.
    Commentary

    In expanding himself into seven forms Krsna was showing Satya that he could enjoy with many women without any loss for her.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After hearing this rule the Lord bound his clothing. It should be understood that he smiled. He bound his clothing tightly, showing he was fully capable (prabhuḥ) or being capable because of previous practice as a cowherd. Expanding his form into seven, he easily subdued the bulls. The word eva can also indicate that it only appeared that he had seven forms, since he moved so quickly.

    • RGovindaSw SB 10-58-45 Telugu - 2012-12-17 ISKCON Tirupati
      His Holiness Rama Govinda Swami· 2012-12-17· Telugu
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    When seven bulls bar one door, Bhagavān does not seek a second door — He becomes seven. Multiplication is not a clever trick; it is the visible form of Kṛṣṇa's plenitude meeting plurality at exactly its own count.

    Stories
    Multiplication during rāsa

    In SB 10.33, when the gopīs began to think themselves uniquely close to Kṛṣṇa, He multiplied — placing one Kṛṣṇa with each gopī, so that every dancer had her own partner. The Bhāgavatam treats this as Bhagavān's plenipotent answer to plurality.

    Gauḍīyas read the seven-Kṛṣṇa subduing of the seven bulls as a kṣatriya-mode echo of that mādhurya-mode multiplication. The same Lord, in a different rasa, answers the same numerical problem with the same solution.

    Important Words
    • dāmabhiḥ — with ropes
      Instrumental plural of dāma — rope. The Dāmodara-word. Gauḍīya: the rope-vocabulary deliberately reverses SB 10.9; the rope that could not bind Him here binds at His pleasure.
    • śauriḥ — Lord Kṛṣṇa (descendant of Śūrasena)
      From Śūrasena, Kṛṣṇa's paternal grandfather. The clan-name surfaces in a moment of warrior valour. Gauḍīya: the Bhāgavatam selects names by rasa — Śauri for the bull-binding episode signals martial register.
    • dāru - mayān — like a child with wooden bulls
      Compound phrase bāla (child) + dāru-maya (made of wood). The Bhāgavatam likens His handling of these terrible bulls to a child dragging wooden toys. Gauḍīya: vātsalya-rasa quietly tints even the kṣatriya scene; Kṛṣṇa is always the child of Vraja somewhere beneath.
    • līlayā — playfully
      Repeated from verse 45 — the act remains līlā. Gauḍīya: the adverb is the doctrine; bhakti's whole answer to 'why does Bhagavān do this?' is līlayā.
    Lord Śauri tied up the bulls, whose pride and strength were now broken, and pulled them with ropes just as a child playfully pulls wooden toy bulls.

    They were like wooden toys pulled by strings by a child.

    Concepts

    Related lectures
    • Padaseva Pr SB 10-58-46 Oriya
      His Grace Padaseva Prabhu· Oriya
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    What broke the pride of every other suitor now becomes a wooden toy in a child's hands — the same animals, the same ropes, but the agent has changed. The dāmodara who could not be tied is here the binder.

    Stories
    Dāmodara at the mortar

    In SB 10.9, Yaśodā tried to bind her toddler to the mortar with cord after cord, and every rope fell two fingers short — until her exhaustion itself became the rope that bound Him. Hence His name Dāmodara: 'rope-bellied'.

    Here the rope-grammar reverses: He who could not be bound easily binds wild bulls and pulls them like wooden toys. Gauḍīyas read the two scenes as one koan — Bhagavān is bound by love alone; nothing else binds Him, and nothing resists Him.

    Important Words
    • vismitaḥ — astonished
      From vi + √smi — wonder-struck. Even the king who set the test is astonished at the answer. Gauḍīya: when Bhagavān answers, the questioner is moved beyond what he asked for. The astonishment is itself part of the gift.
    • vidhi - vat — in the proper Vedic fashion
      Compound vidhi (rule) + -vat (suffix: in accordance with). Bhagavān accepts the bride in śāstric form. Gauḍīya: even after a non-Vedic test (bull-subduing), the marriage itself follows vidhi. Rasa overlays vidhi; vidhi remains intact.
    • sadṛśīm — (this) suitable (bride)
      From sa (together with) + √dṛś (to see) — like, matching. The Bhāgavatam pronounces her sadṛśī — fit for Bhagavān. Gauḍīya: a wife of Kṛṣṇa is by definition fit; the verse names the fitness explicitly.
    Then King Nagnajit, pleased and astonished, presented his daughter to Lord Kṛṣṇa. The Supreme Personality of Godhead accepted this suitable bride in the proper Vedic fashion.
    Purport

    The word sadṛśīm indicates that the lovely princess was a fitting bride for the Lord because she possessed wonderful transcendental qualities that complemented His. As Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī points out, the word vismitaḥ indicates that King Nagnajit was certainly astonished at the many extraordinary events suddenly taking place in his life.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Then King Nagnajit, pleased and astonished, presented his daughter to Lord Kṛṣṇa. The Supreme Personality of Godhead accepted this suitable bride in the proper Vedic fashion.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The king was astonished because suddenly he had attained such good fortune. The Lord married her (prayagṛhṇāt). The wedding was lavish since he was endowed with all wealth (prabhuḥ).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The king was astonished by this direct experience of Kṛṣṇa’s amazing abilities. Or because he was pleased he smiled (vi-smitaḥ) in a special way. Kṛṣṇa accepted the bride or married her who was equal to himself in form and qualities (sadṛśīm) according to the rules because he was capable of fulfilling the desire of his devotee (prabhuḥ), because he manifested all powers (bhagavān).
